---
title: "4.4 Constrained Extrema: Optimizing with a Budget"
---

## The problem

Two reagents are to be mixed for the elementary reaction $\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B} \to \mathrm{P}$,
whose initial rate is $k[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]$. Suppose a solubility limit (or a fixed ionic
strength, or simply the capacity of the apparatus) caps the *total* concentration at
$[\mathrm{A}] + [\mathrm{B}] = C$. How should the budget be divided to get the fastest
possible start?

Section 4.3 taught us to find a maximum by solving $y' = 0$, but it taught us for
a function of *one* variable, and here there are two knobs: $[\mathrm{A}]$ and
$[\mathrm{B}]$. Try to ignore the cap and the question collapses — make both
concentrations bigger and the rate grows without limit, so the unconstrained problem has
no answer at all. It is the **budget that gives the question its meaning**. We have a
quantity to make as large as possible (the *objective*, $q = [\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]$,
which is the rate divided by $k$) and a rule the choices must obey (the *constraint*,
$[\mathrm{A}]+[\mathrm{B}]=C$). This section is about how a constraint turns a two-knob
problem back into one we already know how to solve — and what the solution means.

## One budget removes one knob

The constraint is not an extra complication; it is a *relation* that removes one degree
of freedom. If $[\mathrm{A}]+[\mathrm{B}]=C$, then once you choose $[\mathrm{A}]$,
$[\mathrm{B}]$ is no longer yours to choose: $[\mathrm{B}] = C - [\mathrm{A}]$. Substitute
it into the objective and the two-knob function becomes a one-knob function,
$$q([\mathrm{A}]) = [\mathrm{A}]\,\big(C - [\mathrm{A}]\big),$$
and §4.3 applies unchanged. Geometrically, the allowed choices form a line through the
$[\mathrm{A}]$–$[\mathrm{B}]$ plane, and $q$ restricted to that line is the height of a
landscape measured while walking along it. The *restricted function* is that height
profile; its maximum is the answer.

::: {.env .example}
**Example 4.4.1 — dividing a concentration budget.** With $C = 2.00$ M, find the split
of $[\mathrm{A}]+[\mathrm{B}] = C$ that maximizes the encounter factor $q = [\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]$.

*Setting it up.* One constraint, two variables: eliminate $[\mathrm{B}]$. The domain is
$0 \le [\mathrm{A}] \le C$ (concentrations cannot be negative).

*Solution.* $q([\mathrm{A}]) = C[\mathrm{A}] - [\mathrm{A}]^{2}$, so by the power rule
$$\frac{dq}{d[\mathrm{A}]} = C - 2[\mathrm{A}] = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad [\mathrm{A}] = \frac{C}{2} = 1.00\ \text{M}, \quad [\mathrm{B}] = 1.00\ \text{M}.$$
The second derivative is $d^{2}q/d[\mathrm{A}]^{2} = -2 < 0$: a cap, a maximum. At the
endpoints $q = 0$ (all A or all B means no encounters), so the interior point wins:
$q_{\max} = 1.00\ \text{M}^2$.

*Check.* Units: $q$ is in M². An uneven split $0.5/1.5$ gives $q = 0.75$ M², 25 %
lower — consistent with a maximum at the even split. The result is also physically
sensible: every encounter needs one A *and* one B, so starving either reagent hurts.
:::

::: {.env .remark}
Both panels of the [constrained-extrema studio](constrained-extrema-studio.html) show
exactly this. On the left is the plane with contours of $q$ and the allowed line; on
the right is the height profile along that line. Drag the point along the constraint
and watch the profile's tangent become flat at the even split. Change the total
concentration $C$ and the optimum follows it.
:::

## What the picture says: tangency and parallel gradients

The substitution trick works whenever you can solve the constraint for one variable.
Its geometry, however, carries a deeper statement worth having. Draw the **contours**
of the objective — the curves along which $q$ is constant ($[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}] = 0.4,\,1.0,\,1.7,\dots$,
a family of hyperbolas). Walking along the constraint line, you cross contours, climbing
or descending, until you reach a point where the line merely *grazes* a contour and
turns back: the highest contour you can reach. **At a constrained maximum, the
constraint is tangent to a contour of the objective.** If it crossed the contour, you
could still step to a higher one.

To say this with numbers, we need the vector that points uphill. When a function has two
variables, its slope along each axis is an ordinary derivative with the *other* variable
frozen.

::: {.env .definition}
**Definition 4.4.1 (partial derivative, gradient).** For $f(x,y)$, the *partial
derivative* $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ is the ordinary derivative with respect to
$x$ treating $y$ as a constant, and similarly for $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$. The
*gradient* is the vector
$$\nabla f = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x},\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right),$$
which points in the direction of steepest ascent and is perpendicular to the contour
through that point.
:::

No new rules are involved — only the discipline of knowing which letter is the
variable. For $q = [\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]$: $\partial q/\partial[\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{B}]$
(treat $[\mathrm{B}]$ as a constant multiplier) and $\partial q/\partial[\mathrm{B}] = [\mathrm{A}]$, so
$\nabla q = ([\mathrm{B}],\,[\mathrm{A}])$. For the budget $g = [\mathrm{A}]+[\mathrm{B}]$,
$\nabla g = (1,\,1)$, perpendicular to the constraint line.

::: {.env .theorem}
**Theorem 4.4.1 (parallel gradients).** If $f$ has a maximum or minimum on the curve
$g(x,y) = c$ at an interior point where $\nabla g \neq 0$, then there is a number
$\lambda$ such that
$$\nabla f = \lambda\,\nabla g.$$
:::

::: {.env .proof}
Move along the constraint with unit tangent direction $\mathbf{t}$. When both variables
change, the changes in $f$ from the two knobs add — the same "rates add" logic as in
§4.2 — so the rate of change of $f$ along the curve is the dot product $\nabla f\cdot\mathbf{t}$.
At an extremum of $f$ restricted to the curve, that rate is zero (the first-derivative
condition of §4.3), so $\nabla f \perp \mathbf{t}$. But $g$ is constant along its own
level curve, so likewise $\nabla g \perp \mathbf{t}$. In the plane, two vectors that
are both perpendicular to the same nonzero vector point along the same line; hence
$\nabla f = \lambda\nabla g$ for some number $\lambda$.
:::

The theorem and the substitution method are the *same fact* seen two ways: setting the
derivative along the line to zero is setting $\nabla f\cdot\mathbf{t}$ to zero. At the
optimum of Example 4.4.1, $\nabla q = ([\mathrm{B}],[\mathrm{A}]) = (1.00,\,1.00)$ M
$= \lambda\,(1,1)$, so $\lambda = 1.00$ M $= C/2$. The gradient arrows in the studio
are parallel exactly at the optimum, and visibly *not* parallel anywhere else.

## A second system: how a chain shares a stretch

The even split of Example 4.4.1 might tempt you to believe that "constrained optimum"
means "divide equally." A system with unequal parts corrects that. Two bonds in a chain
(a polymer segment, or a flexible linker between two sites) are stretched so that their
lengths $r_1 + r_2$ must equal a fixed total $L$ — the ends are held. In reduced units
each bond is a spring with its own rest length ($=1$) and stiffness: bond 1 is stiff
and bond 2 is soft,
$$E = (r_1 - 1)^{2} + \tfrac12\,(r_2 - 1)^{2}.$$
How does the chain share the stretch, so as to minimize its total strain energy?

::: {.env .example}
**Example 4.4.2 — sharing a fixed stretch.** For $L = 2.6$, find $r_1$ and $r_2$ that
minimize $E$ subject to $r_1 + r_2 = L$, with each $r_i \ge 0.9$.

*Setting it up.* Eliminate $r_2 = L - r_1$. Then $E(r_1) = (r_1-1)^2 + \tfrac12(L - r_1 - 1)^2$,
with domain $0.9 \le r_1 \le L - 0.9 = 1.7$.

*Solution.* By the chain rule,
$$\frac{dE}{dr_1} = 2(r_1-1) - (L - r_1 - 1) = 3r_1 - L - 1 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; r_1 = \frac{L+1}{3} = 1.20,\quad r_2 = 1.40.$$
$\dfrac{d^{2}E}{dr_1^{2}} = 3 > 0$: a cup, a minimum. Endpoints: $E(0.9) = 0.255$,
$E(1.7) = 0.495$, both above $E_{\min} = (L-2)^2/3 = 0.120$.

*Interpretation and check.* The stiff bond stretches by $r_1 - 1 = 0.20$; the soft one
by $r_2 - 1 = 0.40$. **The stiffer bond takes half the extension of the softer one — the
shares are inversely proportional to stiffness.** The gradient confirms the physics:
$\nabla E = \big(2(r_1-1),\; r_2-1\big) = (0.40,\,0.40) = \lambda(1,1)$, so $\lambda = 0.40$ —
and $0.40$ is *the force in each bond*: springs in series carry the same tension, and
the multiplier turns out to be that shared tension.
:::

In molecular terms this is why strain in a stretched chain concentrates in its softest
link, a first-principles reason behind mechanochemistry. The optimum was not an equal
split, but it was the same procedure: eliminate, differentiate, classify, check the
edges, interpret.

## Does the even split ever win again? A family of cases

Back to the reagents. Real reactions are not all $\mathrm{A}+\mathrm{B}$: an elementary
step $2\mathrm{A}+\mathrm{B}\to\mathrm{P}$ has rate $k[\mathrm{A}]^2[\mathrm{B}]$ and, in general,
$k[\mathrm{A}]^{a}[\mathrm{B}]^{b}$. Keep the budget fixed and change only the exponents:
for which feed ratio is the initial rate largest?

::: {.widget-frame}
::: {.widget-predict}
Before touching anything: for $k[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]^{2}$ with a total of $0.60$ M,
predict the best $[\mathrm{A}]$ and $[\mathrm{B}]$. Then predict what changes for
$[\mathrm{A}]^{2}[\mathrm{B}]$. Is it still an even split? Set the exponents and check.
:::
::: {.widget-body}
<div style="margin-bottom:0.6rem;">
  <label>exponent a <input type="range" id="soA" min="1" max="4" value="1" step="1"></label>
  <label style="margin-left:1rem;">exponent b <input type="range" id="soB" min="1" max="4" value="2" step="1"></label>
  <label style="margin-left:1rem;">total C <input type="range" id="soC" min="0.2" max="2" value="0.6" step="0.05"></label>
</div>
<div style="margin-bottom:0.6rem;">
  <label>[A] on the budget <input type="range" id="soX" min="0" max="1" value="0.15" step="0.005"></label>
  <button id="soPlay" type="button">▶ sweep</button>
</div>
<canvas id="soCanvas" width="640" height="340"></canvas>
<div class="widget-readout" id="soReadout"></div>
:::
::: {.widget-debrief}
The optimum sits at $[\mathrm{A}]^{*} = \dfrac{a}{a+b}\,C$: for $[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]^2$ with
$0.60$ M, $[\mathrm{A}]^* = 0.20$ M and $[\mathrm{B}]^* = 0.40$ M — a $1\!:\!2$ feed, not
$1\!:\!1$. The best mixture is the one in the **stoichiometric ratio** of the
exponents. The gradient condition shows why: $\partial q/\partial[\mathrm{A}] = a\,q/[\mathrm{A}]$
and $\partial q/\partial[\mathrm{B}] = b\,q/[\mathrm{B}]$, and since $\nabla g = (1,1)$ the two must
be equal at the optimum, which forces $[\mathrm{A}]/[\mathrm{B}] = a/b$. Notice the curve
changes *shape* with the exponents — more lopsided, more cusp-like — but it keeps its
single interior peak.
:::
:::

For a termolecular step $2\mathrm{A}+\mathrm{B}$ with a $0.90$ M budget the best feed is
$0.60$ M A and $0.30$ M B: **feed the reagents in the ratio in which the reaction
consumes them.** The even split of Example 4.4.1 was not a general principle but the
special case $a = b = 1$.

## The multiplier is a price

What *is* $\lambda$? It has appeared three times — $1.00$ M for the reagents, $0.40$ for
the chain tension — and each time it was found by comparing gradients. It has a meaning
that checks out in both examples. Relax the budget slightly and ask how much the
*optimal* value improves. For the reagents, the best possible $q$ at total $C$ is
$q^*(C) = C^{2}/4$, so
$$\frac{dq^*}{dC} = \frac{C}{2} = \lambda .$$
At $C = 2.00$ M this is $1.00$ M, exactly the $\lambda$ found before; and a numerical
check agrees ($q^*(1.6) - q^*(1.5) = 0.0775$ over a $0.1$ M change, a rate of $0.775$ — the
value of $\lambda = C/2$ at the midpoint). For the chain, the minimum strain is
$E^*(L) = (L-2)^2/3$, so
$$\frac{dE^*}{dL} = \frac{2(L-2)}{3} = 0.40 \quad\text{at } L = 2.6 = \lambda .$$
Here it is pure physics: the energy cost of stretching the held chain a little further
is force times distance, so $dE^*/dL$ *is* the tension $F$. In both examples
$$\boxed{\;\lambda = \frac{d(\text{optimal value})}{d(\text{budget})}\;}$$
— the **price of the constraint**, the amount the optimum improves per unit of extra
budget. We have verified this in two cases rather than proved it in general, but it
holds in general (it is the *shadow price* of optimization theory). Its units
give it away: $\lambda$ carries (objective units) per (budget units) — M²/M, or
energy per length, which is force.

## The physical payoff: why heat flows until temperatures match

One more system, and the most important in chemistry, because its multiplier is a
quantity you already know. Two bodies exchange energy but are isolated from everything
else, so their energies obey a fixed total $E_1 + E_2 = E$. Statistical mechanics
tells us that a body with $f$ quadratic degrees of freedom has entropy
$S = \tfrac{f}{2}\ln E_i + \text{const}$ (in units of $k_B$) — more energy, more
accessible microstates, with diminishing returns. Write $a = f_1/2$ and $b = f_2/2$.
The system will settle where the *total* entropy is largest:
$$S_{\text{tot}} = a\ln E_1 + b\ln E_2, \qquad E_1 + E_2 = E.$$

Eliminate $E_2 = E - E_1$ and differentiate:
$$\frac{dS_{\text{tot}}}{dE_1} = \frac{a}{E_1} - \frac{b}{E - E_1} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; E_1 = \frac{a}{a+b}\,E .$$
The second derivative $-a/E_1^2 - b/E_2^2 < 0$ confirms a maximum. And the multiplier:
$\nabla S = (a/E_1,\; b/E_2) = \lambda\,(1,1)$, so
$$\frac{a}{E_1} = \frac{b}{E_2} = \lambda .$$
Now recall what $dS/dE$ *means* in thermodynamics: $\dfrac{dS}{dE} = \dfrac{1}{T}$. The two
slopes at the optimum are $1/T_1$ and $1/T_2$, so **$\lambda = 1/T$ and the optimum
is $T_1 = T_2$**: thermal equilibrium is a constrained maximum of entropy, and the
multiplier is the inverse temperature. The split $E_1 = \frac{a}{a+b}E$ gives each
degree of freedom the same energy — **equipartition**, derived from a Lagrange condition.

::: {.widget-frame}
::: {.widget-predict}
Body 1 has $a = 3$ (six modes), body 2 has $a = 2$ (four modes), sharing $E = 10$. Place
body 1 at $E_1 = 8$ (lots of energy). Predict: which body is hotter, and which way
will energy flow? Then press **let heat flow** and watch the temperatures — and
the total entropy — as the system relaxes.
:::
::: {.widget-body}
<div style="margin-bottom:0.6rem;">
  <label>modes a <input type="range" id="ssA" min="1" max="5" value="3" step="1"></label>
  <label style="margin-left:1rem;">modes b <input type="range" id="ssB" min="1" max="5" value="2" step="1"></label>
  <label style="margin-left:1rem;">energy of body 1 <input type="range" id="ssE1" min="0.5" max="9.5" value="8" step="0.05"></label>
  <button id="ssRelax" type="button">▶ let heat flow</button>
</div>
<canvas id="ssCanvas" width="640" height="380"></canvas>
<div class="widget-readout" id="ssReadout"></div>

::: {.widget-debrief}
At $E_1 = 8$ body 1 is the hot one ($T_1 = E_1/a = 2.67 > T_2 = E_2/b = 1.00$): energy flows from
body 1 to body 2, the total entropy climbs, and the two inverse temperatures — the two
tangent slopes — converge until they are equal at $E_1 = 6$, $E_2 = 4$, $T = 2$. Heat
flows from hot to cold *because that is the direction in which total entropy
increases*. The slope bars equalizing is the picture of $\nabla S = \lambda\nabla g$
with $\lambda = 1/T$.
:::
:::

## Remarks and cautions

::: {.env .caution}
**Do not forget the constraint.** Setting *both* partial derivatives of $q$ to zero,
$[\mathrm{B}] = 0$ and $[\mathrm{A}] = 0$, finds the unconstrained stationary point at
the origin, where $q = 0$ — the wrong question's answer. The constraint changes which
points are admissible and which condition characterizes the best one. The right
condition is $\nabla f = \lambda\nabla g$, never $\nabla f = 0$.
:::

::: {.env .caution}
**Parallel gradients find candidates, not verdicts.** Like $y' = 0$ in §4.3, the
condition $\nabla f = \lambda\nabla g$ only says where an extremum *could* be. Classify
it with the second derivative of the restricted function (or with the profile), and
compare the endpoints of the allowed range — a budget has edges (zero concentration, a
bond that cannot compress) where the tangent condition need not hold.
:::

::: {.env .remark}
Read units to identify $\lambda$: it always carries (objective units) per (budget
units). That is M²/M for the reagents, energy per length — a force — for the chain, and
$k_B$ per energy — an inverse temperature — for the heat-sharing bodies. A multiplier
whose units you cannot interpret is usually a signal to recheck the setup.
:::

## Summary

When chemistry fixes a total — of concentration, of length, of energy — two variables
become one, because the constraint removes a degree of freedom: solve it for one
variable, substitute, and the extrema machinery of §4.3 applies to the restricted
function. The geometry behind that algebra is tangency: at a constrained optimum the
constraint grazes a contour of the objective, and the gradients of objective and
constraint, which are both perpendicular to the allowed direction, are parallel, so
$\nabla f = \lambda\nabla g$. The optimum is not generally an even split — it divides the
budget in the stoichiometric ratio for a rate law $[\mathrm{A}]^a[\mathrm{B}]^b$, and
inversely with stiffness for bonds in series — and the multiplier $\lambda$ is the
price of the constraint, the rate at which the optimum improves per unit of extra
budget, which turned out to be a tension for a stretched chain and an inverse
temperature for two bodies sharing energy. What remains open: heat-sharing between two
bodies is the simplest case of a far larger problem. With $10^{23}$ molecules and a
single energy budget, how is the energy most probably distributed among them? The same
optimization, applied to a vast number of variables, yields the Boltzmann distribution —
and that is where the next module goes.
